title.zh: 旧指南针偏了三度，而官方地图却是被故意画错的

description.en: Cartographer Mara Quinn inherits a brass compass that consistently points three degrees west of north. Its apparent flaw leads to altered survey lines…
description.zh: 一根偏斜的指针，把制图师带到一条被人花钱移动的边界。

summary.en: Cartographer Mara Quinn inherits a brass compass that consistently points three degrees west of north. Its apparent flaw leads to altered survey lines, an illegal timber concession and the erased testimony of a mountain community. Correcting the map requires more than exposing fraud; it requires returning authority to the people whose land the map was supposed to describe.
summary.zh: 制图师玛拉·奎因继承了一只总比正北偏西三度的黄铜指南针。这个看似故障的偏差牵出被篡改的测量线、非法伐木许可和被抹去的山地社区证词。纠正地图不只是揭露欺诈，更要把解释土地的权力还给真正生活在那里的人。

warning.en: Fiction. Contains environmental damage, corporate intimidation, historic displacement, document falsification, a wilderness emergency and legal hearings. No graphic violence.
warning.zh: 虚构故事。包含环境破坏、企业恐吓、历史迁移、文件伪造、野外险情及法律听证；无血腥暴力描写。

en: ## Chapter One: Three Degrees West

Mara Quinn inherited her grandfather’s brass compass with a note: It is not broken. Ask what north meant in 1968. The needle settled three degrees west of every calibrated instrument in her survey office.

Her grandfather, Thomas Quinn, had mapped the Alder Range before a hydroelectric reservoir flooded several valleys. Current maps placed the Niska community forest outside its traditional boundary and inside a new timber concession.

Mara assumed the old compass had been magnetized by age. Then she found pencil bearings in Thomas’s field book. When plotted using the compass’s three-degree offset, the lines matched stone markers still described in Niska oral histories.
The official 1968 map used true north everywhere except along the community forest, where the boundary shifted by exactly the same three degrees in the opposite direction.
## Chapter Two: The Line Beneath the Reservoir

Mara met Niska land steward Leah Fox, who refused to treat the notebook as automatic proof. Outside experts had arrived before with discoveries, taken copies and left the community to fight over the consequences.

Together they designed a survey controlled by the Niska council. Elders chose which locations could be visited, young local mappers operated the instruments and all data remained in a community-owned archive.

They located two stone markers above the reservoir and one submerged foundation visible during seasonal low water. Tree-ring dates, historic photographs and Thomas’s bearings placed the original boundary nearly four kilometers east of the official line.

Timber company North Meridian sent Mara a legal notice accusing her of interfering with a valid concession. Her employer asked her to stop using the firm’s equipment. She returned the instruments and continued as an unpaid technical adviser to the council.
## Chapter Three: What Happened in 1968

The provincial archive released closed correspondence after Leah filed an access request. A government survey chief had warned that the reservoir relocation left little time for consultation. North Meridian’s predecessor offered equipment and staff if the boundary could be completed before winter.

One memo instructed drafters to correct a troublesome western bearing so the new concession would form a continuous block. Thomas protested, then signed the final map. His field book showed that he kept the altered compass as a physical reminder of the three-degree change.

Mara struggled with that signature. Her grandfather had preserved evidence, but he had also allowed the false map to govern lives for decades. Leah told her that confession after death was not the same as repair.

They found Thomas’s later letters asking officials to reopen the survey. Each had been filed without action. The letters did not excuse him, but they completed the record of pressure, failure and unfinished responsibility.
## Chapter Four: The Firebreak

Before the hearing, logging crews entered the disputed area under an accelerated permit. A lightning storm then ignited a fire along a cut road. The crews evacuated, while Niska fire guardians used old wetland routes absent from official maps to build a break.

Mara joined the mapping team at the emergency center. The community’s data guided water trucks and protected a stand of old cedar. No one was seriously injured, but the fire exposed how dangerous an inaccurate map could become when agencies treated it as unquestionable truth.

The province suspended logging and opened a public inquiry. North Meridian’s lawyers argued that modern permits could not be undone by a historic drafting decision. Leah answered that the company had renewed the concession repeatedly while ignoring evidence provided by the people living on the land.
Mara presented both the technical survey and her grandfather’s role. She did not turn him into a secret hero. Accuracy required naming the moment he yielded as clearly as the evidence he saved.
## Chapter Five: A Map with More Than One Author

The inquiry voided the disputed concession, recognized the corrected community-forest boundary and ordered compensation for unauthorized harvests. Officials also funded restoration directed by the Niska council rather than by the company that caused the damage.

A new map was published with joint authorship: Niska land stewards, community survey apprentices and independent cartographers. It included both coordinates and traditional place names, while sensitive cultural sites remained in a protected layer controlled by the council.

Mara donated Thomas’s field book to the community archive under terms set by the elders. She kept the compass only until a small exhibition about the survey closed, then returned it as part of the record.

The final display placed the crooked needle beside two maps. Its caption read: An instrument can be wrong by accident. A map becomes a lie when people know the error and benefit from leaving it there.
North had never belonged to the compass alone. It belonged to the people who could explain where they stood, where they had come from and who carried responsibility for drawing the line.
zh: ## 第一章：向西偏三度
制图师玛拉·奎因从祖父那里继承一只黄铜指南针，附带一张纸条：它没有坏，去问问1968年的“北”是什么意思。无论和办公室哪台校准仪器比较，指针都会稳定地向正北偏西三度。
祖父托马斯·奎因曾在水电水库淹没多个山谷前测绘阿尔德山脉。现行地图把尼斯卡社区森林画在传统边界之外，却正好落进一项新伐木许可区。
玛拉起初以为旧指南针只是受年代影响。后来她在托马斯的野外笔记里发现铅笔方位角。按指南针三度偏差绘制后，那些线与尼斯卡口述历史中的石界标完全对应。
1968年的官方地图在所有地方都使用真北，唯独经过社区森林时，边界以相反方向精确移动了三度。
## 第二章：水库下面的边界
玛拉见到尼斯卡土地守护人莉亚·福克斯。莉亚拒绝把笔记自动当成真相，因为过去也有外来专家带着“发现”而来，复制资料后离开，只留下社区承担争议。
她们共同设计一项由尼斯卡议会控制的测量。长者决定哪些地点可以进入，本地年轻制图员操作仪器，所有数据保存在社区拥有的档案中。
团队找到水库上方两个石界标，以及季节性低水位时可见的一处淹没地基。树轮年代、历史照片和托马斯的方位记录共同表明，原边界比官方线向东近四公里。
北方经线木业向玛拉发出律师函，指控她干扰有效许可。雇主要求她停止使用公司设备。她归还全部仪器，以无偿技术顾问身份继续为社区议会工作。
## 第三章：1968年发生的事
莉亚提交信息公开申请后，省档案馆解封一批信件。一名政府测量主管曾警告，水库搬迁让咨询时间严重不足。北方经线的前身公司提出提供设备与人员，条件是边界必须在入冬前完成。
一份备忘录要求绘图员“纠正”那条麻烦的西向方位，使新许可区能够连成一片。托马斯提出反对，最终却仍在地图上签字。他保留偏斜指南针，是为了让三度改变成为无法忽视的实物提醒。
玛拉很难面对那个签名。祖父保存了证据，也让错误地图支配当地生活数十年。莉亚告诉她，死后的解释并不等于真正修复。
她们又找到托马斯后来要求重新测量的信，每一封都被归档而无人处理。这些信不能替他开脱，却补齐了压力、妥协和未完成责任的记录。
## 第四章：防火隔离带
听证前，伐木队依靠加速许可进入争议区域。随后雷暴在运输路旁引发山火。工人撤离，尼斯卡消防守护员则利用官方地图上没有标出的旧湿地路线修筑隔离带。
玛拉加入应急中心制图组。社区数据引导水车进入，保护了一片古老雪松。没有人严重受伤，但火灾证明，当机构把错误地图当成不可质疑的事实时，偏差会变成现实危险。
省政府暂停伐木并启动公开调查。北方经线律师辩称，现代许可不应因一项历史绘图决定被撤销。莉亚回答，公司多次续签许可，却始终无视生活在这片土地上的人提供的证据。
玛拉同时陈述技术测量与祖父的责任。她没有把托马斯塑造成秘密英雄。真正的准确，既要说明他保存了什么，也要清楚写出他在哪一刻选择了退让。
## 第五章：不止一个作者的地图
调查最终撤销争议许可，承认修正后的社区森林边界，并下令赔偿未经授权的采伐。政府还拨款进行生态修复，由尼斯卡议会主持，而不是让造成损害的公司负责。
新地图以联合署名发布：尼斯卡土地守护人、社区测量学徒和独立制图师。图上同时标注坐标与传统地名，敏感文化地点则保存在由议会控制的受保护图层。
玛拉按照长者确定的条件，把托马斯的野外笔记捐给社区档案馆。那只指南针只在测量专题展期间由她保管，闭展后也作为记录的一部分归还。
最终展览把偏斜指针放在两张地图之间。说明牌写着：仪器可能因意外出错；当人们明知错误并从保留错误中获益时，地图才会变成谎言。
北方从来不只属于指南针。它属于那些能够说明自己站在哪里、从哪里来，也能指出究竟由谁为那条边界承担责任的人。
